clue.text: How Billingsgate smells with loch being distant

blocks.note: Billingsgate is London's famous fish market, so it smells 'of fish'
Loch Ness, the best-known Scottish loch

explanation.surface: A comment on the reek of a London fish market, set beside a remote Scottish loch.
explanation.walkthrough: Billingsgate is London's wholesale fish market; read its smell as the phrase OF FISH, then add the loch.
explanation.definitionFit: Offishness is aloofness, the noun for a cool and standoffish manner towards other people.

clue.text: Cloaked in bile, this pearl-clutcher would make lad unproductive

indicators.note: what is cloaked sits inside a covering, so stripping the wrapper away leaves only the hidden core

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
unproductive land or animals are sterile
the wrapper: its letters surround the answer and are removed

explanation.surface: A prudish pearl-clutcher, wrapped in bitterness, would leave a young man unable to father children.
explanation.walkthrough: An unusual reverse construction: the clue describes what you get by wrapping the answer, so you work backwards from the longer word and peel the wrapper away.
explanation.definitionFit: An oyster literally grips a pearl inside its shell; 'pearl-clutcher' is also slang for a shocked prude.

clue.text: Class using the method of ukulele player

blocks.note: a school class is a form
'by' means by means of, as in travel by train

explanation.surface: A lesson that teaches the technique of a famous ukulele strummer.
explanation.walkthrough: George Formby was a hugely popular English comedian and singer of the 1930s-40s, famous for his ukulele songs.
explanation.definitionFit: George Formby, British music-hall star, is remembered above all for strumming the ukulele (strictly a banjolele).

clue.text: Crustacean rests at sea, poked by Woody and Chuck

indicators.note: being all at sea means confused and disordered, so the letters lose their order
something poked has an object pushed into it, so other letters are thrust inside

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
piny means full of pine trees, so wooded
to chuck is to throw, or lob

explanation.surface: A crustacean lies quietly on the seabed, prodded by two characters named Woody and Chuck.
explanation.walkthrough: Woody and Chuck look like names, but are an adjective (piny) and a verb (lob); both go inside the rearranged RESTS, after its first S.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiny lobster, or crawfish, is a clawless marine crustacean with a heavily spined shell.

clue.text: A Christmas Carol very far away from Bleak House, say

indicators.note: what is far away from something is no longer in it, so a letter goes missing

blocks.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
Dickens's Bleak House is an example of a novel, as 'say' signals

explanation.surface: Comparing two Dickens books, A Christmas Carol is said to be nothing like Bleak House.
explanation.walkthrough: Both titles look like Dickens, but A Christmas Carol is the definition read literally: one carol sung at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: A noel is a Christmas carol, from the French word for Christmas used in song refrains.

clue.text: Fitting time of year allowing application of salt etc?

definitions.text: time of year allowing application of salt etc

blocks.note: first meaning: suitable for the time or occasion

blocks.clueFragment: time of year allowing application of salt etc
blocks.note: second, playful meaning: split as a time of year plus a suffix meaning 'can be', it describes food that may be flavoured

explanation.surface: A sensible remark about choosing the right time of year to grit the roads with salt.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: SEASON plus ABLE, able to be seasoned with salt and pepper.
explanation.definitionFit: Seasonable weather or advice is appropriate and timely, suited to the occasion when it arrives.

clue.text: Stoker was so-called black sheep

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Someone who stokes a furnace was nicknamed the family black sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stoker' looks like a furnace worker, but it is the surname of the author of Dracula.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker, the Irish author of Dracula, had that first name, short for Abraham.

clue.text: Chorister ignoring saint represented in oratory

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out of account, so a letter is dropped
to represent is to present again in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: A choirboy who has left out a saint is depicted in a place of prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oratory' looks like a chapel, fitting the chorister, but here it means public speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking, which is what oratory also names.

clue.text: Singer-songwriter Swift eviscerated in main area, LA, with no adult present

indicators.note: to eviscerate is to remove the innards, so only the two outside letters survive
the stated letter must be absent everywhere, so every copy of it is struck out
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so these letters go into the middle

blocks.note: MAIN AREA LA with every A (adult, the film-rating letter) removed
the first and last letters of Swift

explanation.surface: A news-style line about Taylor Swift being savaged at a big Los Angeles venue with no grown-ups there.
explanation.walkthrough: Taylor Swift makes 'Singer-songwriter' look like a description of her, but it is the definition; strip all three As from MAIN AREA LA and put Swift's outer letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A minstrel was a medieval travelling musician who composed and performed his own songs.

clue.text: Forces member to admit Republican immorality, backing famous people

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one set of letters takes the other inside
backing means moving backwards, so the letters run from end to start

blocks.note: famous people are big names
R is the abbreviation for Republican
vice is immoral conduct

explanation.surface: A soldier is made to confess Republican misconduct while supporting celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like supporting the famous people, but it is the signal to turn their word round before the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: A serviceman is a member of the armed forces, the army, navy or air force.

clue.text: Spanish city dumping millions of citrus fruit

indicators.note: to dump something is to get rid of it, so a letter is thrown out

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for millions
a lemon is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A Spanish city's economy offloading millions' worth of oranges and lemons.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as 'citrus fruit dumping millions': the fruit loses its M.
explanation.definitionFit: León is a historic city in north-west Spain, capital of the old kingdom of the same name.

clue.text: Younger blend adapted to operatic setting

indicators.note: something adapted is altered to suit, so the letters are refashioned

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A blend made for younger drinkers has been adjusted to suit an opera production.
explanation.walkthrough: Glyndebourne is a country house in Sussex, England, home to a famous summer opera festival.
explanation.definitionFit: Glyndebourne is the venue of a celebrated annual opera festival held in its own opera house.

clue.text: Early developer in ruins by Rome

indicators.note: something in ruins has been smashed apart, so the letters are broken and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A property developer of old builds among the ancient ruins near Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early developer' suggests a pioneering builder or child, but it is an organism at its earliest stage of growth.
explanation.definitionFit: An embryo is an organism in the first stage of growth, developing before birth or hatching.

clue.text: Try very hard object, one deplorably lacking polish?

blocks.note: an object or aim is a goal
a lout is a crude, ill-mannered person, someone without social polish

explanation.surface: Someone fussing over an unpolished ornament, trying very hard with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lacking polish' reads like an unshined object, but it describes a person's manners.
explanation.definitionFit: To go all out is an idiom for putting maximum effort into something.

clue.text: Some classic metal song

blocks.note: 'some' and 'any' are interchangeable, as in 'have you any?'
something classic is old and established
iron is a metal

explanation.surface: A track by a classic heavy-metal band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classic metal' suggests a rock genre; the answer is an old English music-hall song.
explanation.definitionFit: Any Old Iron is a cockney music-hall number from 1911, a scrap-dealer's cry set to a tune.

clue.text: Stage area banged up face

blocks.note: to stage a play or show is to mount it
A is the abbreviation for area
British slang: someone banged up is in prison, or inside

explanation.surface: An actor in the stage area got his face bashed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banged up face' suggests an injury; banged up is British slang for jailed, which is 'inside'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountain face is one of its steep sides, so the slope or flank is the mountainside.

clue.text: Half for Prometheus topping off double, which he normally drinks?

indicators.note: half of a word is one of its two equal parts, so only the closing five letters stay
taking the top off removes what sits first, so the opening letter is lost

blocks.note: the second half of the ten-letter name, its last five letters
double means dual, twofold

explanation.surface: A barman sets aside half a pint for Prometheus while topping up his double.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example: a regular's standing drink order is 'the usual'.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular who orders 'the usual' at a bar gets his habitual drink without naming it.

clue.text: Con‘s dull Scouse mate flipped at the centre

indicators.note: a flip turns things over, and this one happens only in the middle, swapping the two central letters

blocks.note: drab means dull and colourless
wack is Liverpool (Scouse) slang for a friend or mate

explanation.surface: A dull Liverpudlian friend of a con man turned somersaults in the middle of things.
explanation.walkthrough: In DRABWACK the middle pair BW turns round to WB. 'Con' is a disadvantage, as in pros and cons, not a swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawback is a disadvantage, one of the cons weighed against the pros of a plan.

clue.text: Day wearing strict uniform in more ancient out-of-the-way place

indicators.note: whatever wears clothing is wrapped in it, so the outer letters go round the inner one
a thing in another is enclosed by it, so one letter is placed within the second word

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
strict means harsh, severe
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
more ancient is older

explanation.surface: A day spent in strict uniform at some remote, older outpost.
explanation.walkthrough: Two insertions: D goes into HARSH, and U goes into OLDER. The hard shoulder is the emergency lane at the edge of a British motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard shoulder is the strip beside a motorway where stopped vehicles pull over, out of the traffic's path.

clue.text: One has scaled back scheme after reducing reserve

indicators.note: reducing means cutting down, so the word ends up shorter by its final letter

blocks.note: a scheme is a plan
reserve as coolness of manner is ice

explanation.surface: A company has cut back its plans after running down its reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scaled back' looks like reduced, matching the scheme; it means a creature with scales on its back.
explanation.definitionFit: The plaice is a flatfish whose upper side, its back, is covered in scales.

clue.text: Piece of jewellery cross for the price of rings

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so two letters surround the rest

blocks.note: 'at' gives a price, as in 'at five pounds'
a mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey

explanation.surface: A jeweller trading a crucifix at the same cost as some rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like a crucifix, fitting the jewellery, but it is a hybrid animal.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a charm worn as an ornament, often on a chain, to ward off harm.

clue.text: Awkward week in Yule marred with din

indicators.note: one item in another is held within it, so a letter goes inside the word
something marred is damaged and spoilt, so the letters are knocked out of shape

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for week
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An uncomfortable Christmas week spoilt by constant noise.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion happens first, then everything, din included, is rearranged together; Yule is the old word for Christmastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unwieldy is hard to handle because of its size or shape, so it is clumsy to manage.

clue.text: Precious metal nugget, never quite enough for Ring obsessive

indicators.note: never quite enough means always falling a little short, so each word stops before its last letter

blocks.note: gold is a precious metal
a nugget is a lump

explanation.surface: A hoarder for whom precious-metal nuggets are never enough is fixated on rings.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words lose their last letter. 'Precious' also nods to Gollum's name for the Ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Gollum, in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, is consumed by craving for the One Ring.

clue.text: In France and Germany, to and from river

blocks.note: the French word for 'to' is à
the German word for 'from' is von

explanation.surface: Travelling back and forth between France and Germany along a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Translate in order: 'to' in French, then 'from' in German.
explanation.definitionFit: The Avon is an English river, best known for flowing through Shakespeare's Stratford.

clue.text: Regular participants in quite a hot state

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so only every second letter of the word takes part

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: The usual attendees are in a fairly agitated condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot state' looks like a phrase; 'hot' gives H and 'state' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah is one of the fifty United States, in the American West.

clue.text: One wandering giant almost cuts mate like a saw

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word stops short of its last letter
cutting into something splits it open, so the other letters get wedged inside

blocks.note: a mate is a pal
a rover is one who roams
giant means big

explanation.surface: A wandering giant cuts through his companion as if with a saw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a cutting tool, fitting 'cuts', but it means an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying or proverb, so being like one is being proverbial.

clue.text: Trickster said to be subdued

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so it is the sound and not the spelling that counts

blocks.note: subdued means low-key, quiet and restrained

explanation.surface: A prankster is reputed to be rather quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: Loki is the shape-shifting trickster god of Norse mythology.
explanation.definitionFit: Loki is the mischief-making god of Norse myth, the archetypal divine trickster.

clue.text: Yankee must stop senseless rant, whatever happens

indicators.note: to stop something is to plug it, like a cork in a bottle, so a letter goes inside

blocks.note: inane means senseless
Y is Yankee in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to rant is to vent

explanation.surface: An American must halt a pointless tirade, come what may.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' means plug, as with a stopper, not halt; and 'rant' is a verb meaning to let off steam.
explanation.definitionFit: In any event is an idiom meaning regardless of circumstances, whatever the outcome.
